source: Kowalski (1979) Algorithm = Logic + Control
finding: An algorithm has a logic part (the knowledge used) and a control part (how it is used). Logic fixes meaning. Control only changes efficiency. The same Horn clauses can be run top-down or bottom-up.
numbers: Worked examples: factorial, subset, grandparent, sorting. Naive sort (permutation plus ordered) and quicksort share the logic idea but differ in control.
quote: The logic component determines the meaning of the algorithm whereas the control component only affects its efficiency.
limits: Conceptual paper with hand-worked examples. No benchmark. Kowalski says the split is not always unambiguous.
agent_relevance: Our schema has the same split: the model writes rules (logic), the program controls order and budget (control).

source: Kowalski (1979) Algorithm = Logic + Control, Horn clause section
finding: Horn clauses (one conclusion, many conditions) can be read declaratively (facts about the world) and procedurally (procedure calls). Top-down reduces a goal to subgoals. Bottom-up derives all consequences and can derive irrelevant facts.
numbers: Credits Pat Hayes for 'computation is controlled deduction' and Codd for the same split in databases.
limits: Horn fragment only. No negation yet.
agent_relevance: A Horn rule base is a small checkable form for S2. Forward chaining suits closure checks. Backward chaining suits one goal.

source: Kowalski (1988) The early years of logic programming
finding: First-hand history. Prolog was named in summer 1972 by Colmerauer and Roussel in Marseille. Kowalski and Colmerauer met in 1971 about grammars as logic and resolution as parsing. SL-resolution acts as a top-down parser. Kowalski separates Prolog (the language) from logic programming (the idea).
numbers: 1971 is sometimes given as the year Prolog was born. 1972 for the first system. Article covers up to Dec 1974.
quote: logic programming allows us to view the same knowledge both declaratively and procedurally.
limits: Personal account, biased to Edinburgh. Hayes disputed credit for 'computation is controlled deduction'.
agent_relevance: One rule set has two readings, so we can check rules by running them.

source: Van Emden and Kowalski (1976) The semantics of predicate logic as a programming language
finding: Gave the least-fixpoint semantics for Horn programs: the meaning is the smallest set of facts closed under the rules. Operational and model-theoretic meanings agree.
numbers: Not opened. Claim from memory; cited by the Kowalski 1979 and 1988 texts.
limits: Not read directly.
agent_relevance: A precise definition of 'all consequences' for a rule set; usable for a completeness check.

source: Clark (1978) Negation as failure
finding: Proposed that a goal that cannot be proved is treated as false (closed world), justified by completing the program.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Not read directly. Gives non-monotonic answers: adding a fact can remove a conclusion.
agent_relevance: Boundary rule: 'not provable' is not 'false'. Label closed-world versus open-world answers.

source: Gelfond and Lifschitz (1988) The stable model semantics for logic programming
finding: Defined stable models for programs with negation. Answer set programming grew from this. A program can have zero, one or many answer sets.
numbers: File downloaded as PostScript but not read (no converter).
limits: Not read directly.
agent_relevance: ASP fits constraint and puzzle problems. Many answer sets map to several candidate worlds.

source: Horrocks and Sattler (2003) Decidability of SHIQ with complex role inclusion axioms
finding: The description logic SHIQ plus unrestricted role inclusion axioms is undecidable, even for restricted forms. Decidability is regained by making the axioms acyclic, with a tableau algorithm.
numbers: Motivation: medical terminology, e.g. propagating a property along a part-of relation. Related: a grammar-logic problem is ExpTime-complete (Demri 2001).
limits: Theory result. Shows the price of expressive power in DLs.
agent_relevance: The richer the rule language, the less we can promise a check will finish. Prefer a decidable fragment (Horn, Datalog, small DL).

source: Clark, Tafjord, Richardson (2020) Transformers as soft reasoners over language (RuleTaker)
finding: Transformers trained on synthetic facts-and-rules text answer true/false questions like a theorem prover. They generalise to deeper chains than seen in training.
numbers: About 99% on the synthetic test. 95%+ at deeper depth. 98% on crowd-paraphrased rules. 90%+ zero shot on 5 of 6 variants of two hand-authored rule bases. Depth-2-trained model: 71.1% at depth 3. Depth-3-trained model: 97.6% at depth 5. Flip test: 81% of expected true-to-false flips occurred after removing a needed sentence.
limits: Trained models, not prompted. Synthetic data. Closed-world negation variants. Robustness to perturbation only moderate (81%).
agent_relevance: Rule text can be reasoned over, but a trained soft prover is not a checker. Verify with a real engine.

source: Tafjord, Dalvi Mishra, Clark (2021) ProofWriter
finding: Generates implications and proofs by iterating a 1-step inference generator. Proofs reflect real model decisions. Also does restricted abduction.
numbers: Proof accuracy beats earlier methods by +9% absolute (abstract). Abstract-level figures only; table cells were garbled in extraction.
limits: Exact table cells not recorded.
agent_relevance: Iterating one small step and checking each step matches our one-operator-per-step design.

source: Saparov and He (2023) Language models are greedy reasoners (PrOntoQA)
finding: InstructGPT and GPT-3 make correct single deduction steps even in fictional or counterfactual ontologies. They fail at proof planning: when several valid steps exist they pick a misleading one and then fail to finish.
numbers: Models ada to text-davinci-002, greedy decoding. Only text-davinci-002 did well on multi-step proofs. Label accuracy correlated poorly with strict proof accuracy. Models were much less misled with a true ontology.
quote: they have difficulty with proof planning: When multiple valid deduction steps are available, they are not able to systematically explore the different options.
limits: Old models (2022). Synthetic ontologies. Results also held with self-consistency and depth-first-trace prompts.
agent_relevance: Strong support for splitting the work: model does steps, program does search. Check the proof, not only the label.

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM: empowering LLMs with symbolic solvers
finding: LLM translates a problem into a logic form. A solver (Pyke logic programming, Prover9, Z3, CSP solver) reasons. Self-refinement fixes solver errors.
numbers: GPT-4 accuracy standard/CoT/Logic-LM: PrOntoQA 77.40/98.79/83.20; ProofWriter 52.67/68.11/79.66; FOLIO 69.11/70.58/78.92; LogicalDeduction 71.33/75.25/87.63; AR-LSAT 33.33/35.06/43.04. ChatGPT average gain 39.2% over standard and 18.4% over CoT. GPT-4 gain 24.98% over standard and 10.44% over CoT.
limits: On PrOntoQA GPT-4 CoT (98.79) beat Logic-LM (83.20). GPT-4 executable rate FOLIO 79.9%, AR-LSAT 32.6% before refinement. Failed parses fall back to CoT.
agent_relevance: Gains come from correct translation, not solving. Real-world text (FOLIO, AR-LSAT) is where translation breaks.

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM, depth and refinement analysis
finding: On ProofWriter the Logic-LM edge over CoT grows with proof depth. Self-refinement raises executable rate but gains flatten.
numbers: Logic-LM minus CoT: +7.1, +5.0, +12.7, +20.0, +39.4 points at depth 0, 1, 2, 4, 5. Self-refinement raised executable rate by 5.01 points on average. GPT-4 FOLIO exec rate 79.9 to 85.8; AR-LSAT 32.6 to 39.8.
limits: Gain at low depth is small. Few extra points after the first refinement rounds.
agent_relevance: Use the engine for deep chains. Use few repair rounds, with solver error text as the signal (fits G2).

source: Olausson et al. (2023) LINC: first-order logic with LLM parsers and Prover9
finding: LLM translates to first-order logic and Prover9 decides. Large gain for small models and for synthetic ProofWriter. For GPT-4 on FOLIO it did not beat CoT.
numbers: FOLIO: StarCoder+ 56.0% LINC vs 41.8% CoT. GPT-3.5 62.6% vs 54.9%. GPT-4 CoT 75.3% vs LINC 72.5%, McNemar p=0.58 (not significant). ProofWriter: GPT-3.5 96.4% and GPT-4 98.3% with LINC. FOL syntax error rates 38% (StarCoder+), 24% (GPT-3.5), 13% (GPT-4).
limits: FOLIO is real-world text. FOL missed implicit facts; merging 'Nazi German politician' into one symbol lost information. LINC predicted Uncertain 57% of the time vs CoT 41%.
agent_relevance: Translation fidelity is the bottleneck. A solver's Uncertain can mean the encoding is incomplete; treat it as a signal to check.

source: Olausson et al. (2023) LINC, error and complementarity analysis
finding: LINC and CoT fail in different ways. LINC is precise when it says True or False.
numbers: LINC precision on True/False 93% vs CoT 81%, recall 60% vs 75%. Predictions: CoT 32% True, 27% False, 41% Uncertain; LINC 24%, 17%, 57%, 2% errors. With StarCoder+, baselines stay near chance as proof depth rises; LINC stays far above chance.
limits: No tested ensemble of the two in this paper.
agent_relevance: Fits G4: different error types are better evidence than agreement of same-type samples.

source: Ye et al. (2023) SatLM: satisfiability-aided language models
finding: LLM writes a declarative spec; a SAT/SMT solver finds the answer. Beats program-aided LMs (imperative code) on constraint-heavy tasks.
numbers: GSM-SYS subset: +23% over ProgLM; 69.4% greedy and 80.9% self-consistency. GSM: 84.8% self-consistency (+2.4 over ProgLM). LSAT SoTA 30.9 to 37.4. BoardgameQA 73.9 to 80.7. Regex synthesis 37.1 (ProgLM) vs 44.0.
limits: On plain GSM with greedy decoding it was slightly worse than ProgLM. On GSM-SYS it answers less often but is more accurate when it answers (77% vs 45%).
agent_relevance: Declare the rules, do not script the steps. Abstention when the solver finds no model is a useful signal.

source: Ishay, Yang, Lee (2023) Leveraging LLMs to generate answer set programs
finding: GPT-3 and GPT-4 turn logic puzzles into answer set programs in a step-by-step few-shot pipeline. Solving directly is much worse. Remaining errors are small and easy for humans to fix.
numbers: 50 train and 100 test puzzles (Mitra and Baral 2015). Test accuracy: zero-shot GPT-3 2%; few-shot GPT-3 3%; zero-shot GPT-4 21%; few-shot GPT-4 7%; GPT-3 ASP 81%; GPT-4 ASP 92%. Supervised baseline LOGICIA 71%.
limits: One puzzle set, small N. Prompts tuned on the 50 training puzzles. Few-shot GPT-4 (7%) was worse than zero-shot GPT-4 (21%).
agent_relevance: Constraint puzzles map well to ASP. The fix-small-errors loop fits G2.

source: Borazjanizadeh and Piantadosi (2024) Reliable reasoning beyond natural language
finding: New 55-problem Non-Linear Reasoning set (21 math word problems, 17 constraint problems, 17 algorithmic games). LLM writes Prolog; the interpreter solves. Large gains when variables depend on many others.
numbers: Navigate: all models above 98% with Prolog, lower with text CoT. NLR: GPT-4 from as low as 8.3% to 100% on two of three categories. Algorithmic games 66.7% vs 8%. Text-only GPT-4 falls from 100% to 0% as interdependence goes 1 to 4; Prolog stays stable.
limits: Only 55 hand-made problems. Uses multiple tries until code is valid. Navigate changed from yes/no to distance to avoid 50% guessing.
agent_relevance: Supports giving state tracking to a Prolog engine rather than the model.

source: Lyu et al. (2023) Faithful Chain-of-Thought reasoning
finding: Two stages: LLM translates the question to symbolic language (Python, Datalog, PDDL); a deterministic solver answers. The chain is faithful by construction. Datalog used for multi-hop QA and relation tasks.
numbers: 10 datasets, code-davinci-002. Greedy: best on 8 of 10. Relative gains up to 14.2% (math word problems), 3.4% (planning), 6.5% (Date), 21.4% (CLUTRR). Small gains on easy sets (0.3 to 2.4%). With GPT-4 over 95% on 4 of 5 math sets and 2 of 3 multi-hop sets.
limits: StrategyQA (Datalog) not better than CoT: hard part is knowledge retrieval, not reasoning. Exact table cells garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Rule engines help when the task is reasoning-limited, not knowledge-limited.

source: Fang et al. (2024) Large language models are neurosymbolic reasoners
finding: LLM agent in text games calls symbolic modules (math, sorting, map navigation) as actions. Average 88% across the symbolic-task games.
numbers: 100 unseen games per task. Average 88%. Compared with RL and behavior-cloning baselines with and without modules.
limits: Modules are arithmetic, sort, navigation, not logic programs. Per-game cells not recorded.
agent_relevance: Supports calling a checked module per rule class instead of free text.

source: Kirtania et al. (2024) Logic-LM++
finding: Improves Logic-LM refinement: the LLM compares two candidate fixes pairwise and keeps the better one. Plain refinement often fixes syntax but adds a semantic error.
numbers: GPT-4 columns standard/CoT/Logic-LM/Logic-LM++: FOLIO 69.11/70.58/78.92/84.80; ProofWriter 52.67/68.11/79.66/79.66; AR-LSAT 33.33/35.06/43.04/46.32. Abstract: +18.5% over standard, +12.3% over CoT, +5% over Logic-LM.
limits: Same ProofWriter score as Logic-LM. Refinement can reintroduce errors (example: 'No young person teaches').
agent_relevance: Repair needs a check on meaning, not only syntax. Compare against held-out cases (G3).

source: Poulis, Tsalapati, Koubarakis (2024) Transformers in the service of description logic-based contexts (DELTAD)
finding: 384K-example dataset in the description logic ALCQ (some, all, at least, at most). A fine-tuned DeBERTa learns it. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 improve with 9 shots but fall off with depth.
numbers: DeBERTa average 97.5%, up to 99.7% at max depth; look-up questions 99.0%. GPT-4 9-shot by depth D=0..5: 89, 86, 77, 80, 83, 83. GPT-4 0-shot D=2..5: 42, 32, 30, 40. Chance 33.3%.
limits: GPTs only on linguistic complexity L<=1 (context limit); N=100 per cell. The fine-tuned model failed 'A and B implies A or B' and said unknown for number restrictions (24 of 29 handcrafted correct).
agent_relevance: Open-world 'unknown' is hard. DLs are open-world, Prolog is closed-world. Label which applies.

source: Poulis et al. (2024) DELTAD, symbolic-form test
finding: When text uses DL words (exists, is subsumed by) instead of plain English, accuracy collapses. Meaningless names cost little; formal wording costs a lot.
numbers: DeBERTa on SoftSymbolic (meaningless names) 95.3%; on HardSymbolic (DL terms) 58.5%. GPT-3.5 0-shot 57%, 9-shot 61%; GPT-4 0-shot 20%, 9-shot 65% on HardSymbolic.
limits: Small test samples (100 for GPTs).
agent_relevance: Formal-looking input is not easier. Test the rule format against the model.

source: OntoURL (2025) benchmark of LLMs on ontological understanding, reasoning, learning
finding: 57,303 questions, 15 tasks. Open models read definitions well and do poorly on description logic reasoning and building ontologies.
numbers: Qwen2.5-72B: constraint reasoning 93.4, instance class reasoning 77.5, SWRL rule reasoning 75.6, description logic reasoning 68.4. Qwen2.5-3B DL reasoning 51.1. Ontology construction tasks L2 to L4 scored about 0 to 22 for most models.
limits: Open-weight models. DL reasoning is true/false so chance is 50%.
agent_relevance: Whole-ontology generation is weak. Keep rule sets small and checked.

source: Brachman and Levesque (1984) Tradeoff between expressiveness and tractability
finding: Founding result: richer representation languages make inference harder. Motivates restricted languages such as description logics.
numbers: Not opened (URL returned an HTML stub).
limits: From memory; not verified.
agent_relevance: Choose the weakest rule language that works.

source: Baader et al. (2003) The Description Logic Handbook
finding: Description logics are decidable fragments of first-order logic with concepts and roles, and open-world reasoning. They underlie OWL.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: From memory.
agent_relevance: Use for class-and-property knowledge; use Datalog or Prolog for rule chaining.
